Slide 3

Recall — Classes 15 and 16

Slide 4
  1. Class 15 — PKI: a certificate is a public key plus an identity, signed by a CA (Certificate Authority) (Certificate Authority). A browser trusts a site when the certificate chains to a root it already trusts and the name matches.
  2. Class 15 — a self-signed certificate is its own issuer: no third party vouches for it, so a client trusts it only after the certificate is installed or its fingerprint is checked.
  3. Class 16 — a VPN builds an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network; WireGuard authenticates each peer by its public key and encrypts every packet with AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data).
  4. Class 16 — encryption in transit protects data while it moves. It does nothing for a file sitting on a disk, which is today's first subject.
  5. LAB_06 Part 1 (the tunnel) was prepared last class; Part 1 and Part 2 are both performed today, with the kit distributed in the work period after the break.

Today's question

Three questions open today, one per lesson. One: a laptop from NorthMaple is lost at an airport — the thief has the disk; what stops them reading the client files? Two: the internal intranet still runs over plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) (Hypertext Transfer Protocol); how do we move it to HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) on one afternoon, with no public Certificate Authority? Three: once the folder is encrypted, the tunnel is up and the service is on HTTPS, how do we prove it — with evidence a second person can check — rather than simply believing it?

Lesson 1 — Encryption of stored dataLocal disks, containers and files; cloud server-side and client-side encryption; keys and recovery; what encryption at rest does and does not protect.
Lesson 2 — Applying certificates to servicesEnabling HTTPS on one internal service with a self-signed certificate: the key, the certificate, the HTTPS-only configuration, distributing trust.
Lesson 3 — Validating that encryption is really in placeProving the three results — stored data unreadable, service HTTPS-only, tunnel encrypted — with repeatable tests, positive controls and recorded evidence.

1.1Data at rest, and what encrypting it does

Slide 6 Slide 7

Key terms

Data at rest — Data stored on a medium that is not currently being processed — a disk, file, backup or cloud object; its encryption on end-user devices is covered by NIST SP 800-111.

Encryption of stored data — Transforming stored bytes with a cipher and a key so the medium holds unreadable ciphertext instead of plaintext.

AES — Advanced Encryption Standard (FIPS 197): the standard symmetric cipher; XTS mode for disks, GCM mode for files.

Threat it answers — Someone obtaining the medium while the system is off or locked: lost laptop, pulled disk, copied backup, stolen snapshot.

Limit — It protects nothing on a running, unlocked system — authorized programs and their malware read decrypted data; it is not a substitute for access control.

1.2Where the encryption happens: five layers

Slide 8 Slide 9

Key terms

Full-disk / volume encryption — Encrypts every sector below the file system: BitLocker (XTS-AES 128, raisable to 256), LUKS2 (aes-xts-plain64), FileVault.

Encrypted container — One file that mounts as a drive when unlocked and is one opaque file when locked: VeraCrypt (AES-XTS).

File / archive encryption — Encrypts selected items or one archive: 7-Zip (AES-256), GnuPG, age.

Complementary controls — Encryption at rest and in transit are not alternatives; a file can be encrypted on disk and travel in the VPN.

Encrypt empty first — Encrypting a used disk does not instantly erase old plaintext from spare sectors; create a fresh container and write into it.

1.3Keys, recovery, and erase

Slide 10 Slide 11 Slide 12

Key terms

Envelope encryption — A DEK encrypts the data; one or more KEKs wrap the DEK, each wrapped copy kept in a key slot.

DEK / KEK — Data Encryption Key encrypts data; Key Encryption Key encrypts (wraps) the DEK.

PBKDF2 (salt, iterations) — Turns a passphrase into a KEK; the salt diversifies the key per system, the iteration count sets a fixed cost per guess.

Recovery password — A separately stored secret (BitLocker: 48 digits) that opens the data if a passphrase is lost; never kept with the data.

Cryptographic erase — Destroying every wrapped copy of the DEK so the ciphertext can never be decrypted (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2).

1.4Encryption in cloud storage

Slide 13

Key terms

Shared responsibility model — The provider secures the infrastructure; the customer configures protection of their data, including encryption.

Server-side encryption — The provider encrypts stored objects and disks: S3 SSE-S3 (default since 2023), SSE-KMS; Azure Storage encryption (always on, AES-256).

SSE-C blocked — S3 server-side encryption with customer-provided keys is blocked by default for new general-purpose buckets since April 6, 2026.

Client-side encryption — Encrypting on the company computer before upload, so the provider cannot read the data: Cryptomator, age, GnuPG.

Cloud envelope — Server-side encryption wraps a per-object DEK under a KMS key that never leaves the service; rotating the KMS key re-protects without re-encrypting.

◎Real-life example

Slide 14
Task

Build NorthMaple's encrypted "vault" for its client-records folder, with a recoverable key, and prove the data is unreadable without it.

▸ Feeds a future lab: LAB_06 Part 2, data-at-rest deliverable (Chapter 6 of the Final Project, 2 of 15 points; Chapter 6 of the Course Procedure Manual, 1 of 10 points).

How it relates to this lecture. This is Lesson 1 made concrete. It performs the data-at-rest part of LAB_06 Part 2 ("one folder or volume of company data encrypted with a free tool") and produces the evidence that Lesson 3 will validate. The vault, its recovery password and the before/after measurements become the files you attach to Chapter 6 of the Final Project and section 6.4 of the Course Procedure Manual.

NorthMaple keeps a folder of client records — a quarterly ledger, corporate-tax notes, a payroll summary — on the file server NM-FS01 (Servers zone, 192.168.20.10) and copies it to a backup disk that leaves the building. The owner asks a direct question: if that backup disk is lost, can the finder read the records? Today you answer it by building an encrypted vault the way BitLocker, LUKS2 and VeraCrypt build one — a single random DEK that encrypts every file with AES-256-GCM, wrapped under two key slots (a passphrase and a 48-digit recovery password) — and then measuring the result: the marker string NORTHMAPLE-CONFIDENTIAL is readable in the plaintext and gone from the ciphertext, a wrong passphrase is refused, the recovery password still works, and changing one bit of a file is detected.

DeliverableThe vault folder (encrypted files plus the header), the offline recovery-password file, and the before/after entropy and marker measurements — the data-at-rest evidence for Chapter 6.
Where it goesLAB_06 Part 2, data-at-rest deliverable (Chapter 6 of the Final Project, 2 of 15 points; Chapter 6 of the Course Procedure Manual, 1 of 10 points).

⌨Code that illustrates the example

Slide 15

The script below is the recorded run that produced the numbers used all through this lesson. Each line is preceded by a full comment; press ▶ Start, then Step and ❚❚ Pause to walk through it with the class while the visualization on the right shows what is happening.

nm_envelope_vault.pyPython 3 with the cryptography package
What it does. Create the fictional client-records folder, encrypt it with envelope encryption (one DEK, two key slots), and run the six proofs: plaintext readable, ciphertext unreadable, wrong passphrase refused, recovery works, tampering detected, passphrase change re-wraps the key only. Link with the lecture. It performs the real-life example end to end and illustrates every term of sub-topics 1.1 and 1.3: DEK, KEK, key slot, PBKDF2, salt, AES-256-GCM, recovery password and cryptographic erase. It is the same envelope pattern BitLocker and LUKS2 use; the HTML player reproduces this recorded run step by step.
ready
1#!/usr/bin/env python3
2# nm_envelope_vault.py - Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB), Class 17, Lesson 1 example.
3# TASK: encrypt a copy of NorthMaple Accounting Inc.'s (fictional) client-records folder
4# the way disk-encryption tools (BitLocker, LUKS2, VeraCrypt) and cloud key services
5# (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault) do it - envelope encryption - and then prove the result.
6# LAB ONLY: run it inside your own isolated laboratory VM (Legal Notice v1.0, section 3).
7# Requirements: Python 3.10 or newer and the "cryptography" package (pip install cryptography).
8# Usage: python3 nm_envelope_vault.py (it creates every file it needs in the current folder)
9
10# Import the standard-library modules: os gives cryptographic random bytes, time measures durations, json writes the vault header, math computes entropy, hashlib computes SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) digests and PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2), pathlib handles folders and files, secrets draws random digits.
11import os, time, json, math, hashlib, pathlib, secrets
12# Import AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode): the authenticated cipher that encrypts each file and detects any change to it.
13from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
14# Import AES Key Wrap (RFC 3394), the standard method for encrypting one key with another key, and the error it raises when the unwrapping key is wrong.
15from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.keywrap import aes_key_wrap, aes_key_unwrap, InvalidUnwrap
16# Import the error AES-GCM raises when an authentication tag does not match (wrong key or modified data).
17from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag
18# The lab-only passphrase of the vault: it exists only in this laboratory exercise and must never be reused anywhere real.
19PASSPHRASE = b"LAB-ONLY Maple-Vault 2026!"
20# The marker string placed at the top of every record: finding it in a file later proves that the file is readable plaintext.
21MARKER = b"NORTHMAPLE-CONFIDENTIAL"
22# The PBKDF2 iteration count: 500,000 rounds of HMAC-SHA-512, the count VeraCrypt uses for non-system volumes; every password guess costs the same work.
23ITERATIONS = 500_000
24# The two working folders: the plaintext source, and the vault that will hold only ciphertext plus its header.
25SRC, VAULT = pathlib.Path("ClientRecords_demo"), pathlib.Path("ClientRecords_vault")
26# Define a function that measures Shannon entropy in bits per byte: 8.0 means all 256 byte values are equally frequent (random-looking); plain text usually scores 4 to 5.
27def entropy(data):
28 # Count how many times each of the 256 possible byte values appears.
29 counts = [0] * 256
30 # Walk through the data one byte at a time and add one to the counter of that byte value.
31 for b in data: counts[b] += 1
32 # Apply Shannon's formula: the sum, over every byte value present, of -p x log2(p), where p is the share of that value.
33 return -sum(c / len(data) * math.log2(c / len(data)) for c in counts if c)
34# Define a function that turns a secret (passphrase or recovery password) into a 256-bit KEK (Key Encryption Key) with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-512 and a salt.
35def derive_kek(secret, salt):
36 # Run 500,000 rounds of HMAC-SHA-512 over the secret and the salt and keep 32 bytes (256 bits) as the KEK.
37 return hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha512", secret, salt, ITERATIONS, dklen=32)
38# Define a short key fingerprint: the first 16 hexadecimal characters of the key's SHA-256 digest; it identifies a key without revealing it.
39def fp(key):
40 # Hash the key and keep a short prefix; printing a fingerprint instead of the key keeps the key secret.
41 return hashlib.sha256(key).hexdigest()[:16]
42# Define the unlock procedure: derive the KEK from a candidate secret and the slot's salt, then try to unwrap the DEK stored in that slot.
43def unlock(secret, slot):
44 # AES Key Wrap checks an integrity value while unwrapping; with a wrong KEK it raises InvalidUnwrap instead of returning a key.
45 return aes_key_unwrap(derive_kek(secret, bytes.fromhex(slot["salt"])), bytes.fromhex(slot["wrapped_dek"]))
46# Confirm that the tools are loaded and show the settings.
47print(f"Tools loaded. Cipher AES-256-GCM, key derivation PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 x {ITERATIONS:,} rounds, key wrap AES-KW (RFC 3394).")
48
49# Create the plaintext source folder (no error if it already exists).
50SRC.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
51# Start an empty dictionary that maps each file name to its content.
52records = {}
53# The quarterly ledger: 120 invented client lines in CSV (Comma-Separated Values) format.
54records["ledger_2026-Q3.csv"] = b"client_id,client_name,period,amount_cad\n" + b"".join(b"NM-C-%04d,Fictional Client %03d Inc.,2026-Q3,%d.%02d\n" % (1000 + i, i, 1200 + 53 * i, (7 * i) % 100) for i in range(120))
55# The tax-return notes: 50 invented lines of the kind an accountant keeps for each T2 corporate return.
56records["tax_notes_T2.txt"] = b"".join(b"Client NM-C-%04d: T2 return reviewed, instalments of %d.00 CAD confirmed, filing due 2027-%02d-30.\n" % (1000 + i, 400 + 25 * i, 1 + i % 6) for i in range(50))
57# The payroll summary: 150 invented employee lines (no real person, no real salary).
58records["payroll_summary.csv"] = b"employee_id,role,gross_cad\n" + b"".join(b"NM-E-%03d,%s,%d.00\n" % (i, [b"accountant", b"technician", b"receptionist"][i % 3], 2100 + 85 * i) for i in range(150))
59# Write every file into the source folder with the marker on its first line, and print its name, size and SHA-256 digest.
60for name, body in records.items():
61 # Put the marker line in front of the content.
62 content = MARKER + b"\n" + body
63 # Write the bytes to disk.
64 (SRC / name).write_bytes(content)
65 # Print the file name, its size in bytes and the first 16 characters of its SHA-256 digest (its identity for later comparison).
66 print(f" {name:<22} {len(content):>6} bytes sha256 {hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest()[:16]}")
67
68# For every source file, compute the entropy and search for the marker.
69for name in records:
70 # Read the file back from disk, as anyone who copied the disk could.
71 data = (SRC / name).read_bytes()
72 # Print the entropy (about 4 to 5 bits per byte for text) and the result of the marker search.
73 print(f" {name:<22} entropy {entropy(data):.3f} bits/byte marker {'FOUND' if MARKER in data else 'not found'}")
74
75# Ask the operating system's cryptographic random generator for 32 bytes (256 bits): this DEK encrypts the data itself.
76dek = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
77# Print only the fingerprint of the DEK; the key itself is never printed and never written to disk in clear.
78print(f"DEK created: 256 bits, fingerprint {fp(dek)} (the key itself is never shown)")
79
80# Create the vault folder that will receive the encrypted files.
81VAULT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
82# Create the AES-256-GCM cipher object with the DEK.
83aead = AESGCM(dek)
84# Prepare the list that describes each encrypted file in the vault header.
85manifest = []
86# Encrypt the files one by one.
87for name in records:
88 # Draw a fresh 96-bit nonce (number used once) for this file: GCM must never reuse a nonce with the same key.
89 nonce = os.urandom(12)
90 # Encrypt the plaintext; the file name is passed as AAD (Additional Authenticated Data), so a renamed or swapped file is detected.
91 ct = aead.encrypt(nonce, (SRC / name).read_bytes(), name.encode())
92 # Write nonce + ciphertext + the 16-byte authentication tag into a .nmv file inside the vault.
93 (VAULT / (name + ".nmv")).write_bytes(nonce + ct)
94 # Add the file to the manifest with the SHA-256 digest of exactly what was written.
95 manifest.append({"file": name + ".nmv", "sha256": hashlib.sha256(nonce + ct).hexdigest()})
96 # Print the sizes: the encrypted file is 12 (nonce) + plaintext + 16 (tag) bytes long.
97 print(f" {name + '.nmv':<26} {len(nonce + ct):>6} bytes = 12 nonce + {len(ct) - 16} ciphertext + 16 tag sha256 {manifest[-1]['sha256'][:16]}")
98
99# For every encrypted file, compute the entropy and search for the marker.
100for entry in manifest:
101 # Read the encrypted file exactly as it sits on disk.
102 data = (VAULT / entry["file"]).read_bytes()
103 # Print the entropy (close to 8.0) and the marker search result (it must not be found).
104 print(f" {entry['file']:<26} entropy {entropy(data):.3f} bits/byte marker {'FOUND' if MARKER in data else 'not found'}")
105
106# Draw a random 128-bit salt for key slot 0: the salt makes the same passphrase produce a different KEK in every vault.
107salt0 = os.urandom(16)
108# Note the start time, to measure how long one derivation takes: this is the cost an attacker pays for every single guess.
109t0 = time.perf_counter()
110# Derive the KEK of slot 0 from the passphrase and its salt.
111kek0 = derive_kek(PASSPHRASE, salt0)
112# Print the duration of one derivation and the fingerprint of the KEK.
113print(f"KEK derived in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s from the passphrase and salt {salt0.hex()[:8]}... -> fingerprint {fp(kek0)}")
114
115# Encrypt the 32-byte DEK with the KEK using AES Key Wrap: the result is 40 bytes and carries its own integrity check.
116slot0 = aes_key_wrap(kek0, dek)
117# Print the size and the beginning of the wrapped key; a wrapped key is safe to store because it is useless without the KEK.
118print(f"Slot 0 (passphrase): wrapped DEK = {len(slot0)} bytes, begins {slot0.hex()[:16]}...")
119
120# Build a 48-digit recovery password from random digits, written in eight groups of six (the layout BitLocker uses for its recovery passwords).
121recovery = "-".join("%06d" % secrets.randbelow(1_000_000) for _ in range(8))
122# Draw a separate random salt for slot 1.
123salt1 = os.urandom(16)
124# Wrap the same DEK with a KEK derived from the recovery password: two different secrets now open the same data.
125slot1 = aes_key_wrap(derive_kek(recovery.encode(), salt1), dek)
126# Save the recovery password in its own file, to be printed and stored offline, never next to the vault.
127pathlib.Path("RECOVERY-PASSWORD_store-offline.txt").write_text(recovery + "\n")
128# Print a masked copy: only the last group of digits appears on screen.
129print("Slot 1 (recovery): recovery password " + "######-" * 7 + recovery[-6:] + " saved to RECOVERY-PASSWORD_store-offline.txt")
130
131# Assemble the header: algorithms, iteration count, each slot's salt and wrapped DEK in hexadecimal, and the manifest (nothing secret in clear).
132header = {"format": "NMV1", "cipher": "AES-256-GCM", "kdf": "PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512", "iterations": ITERATIONS, "slots": [{"name": "passphrase", "salt": salt0.hex(), "wrapped_dek": slot0.hex()}, {"name": "recovery", "salt": salt1.hex(), "wrapped_dek": slot1.hex()}], "files": manifest}
133# Write the header as vault.json in the vault folder.
134(VAULT / "vault.json").write_text(json.dumps(header, indent=2))
135# Drop the program's references to the plaintext keys: from now on the vault is locked (real tools also wipe locked memory, which Python cannot guarantee).
136del dek, kek0, aead
137# Print the content of the vault folder.
138print("Vault locked. Contents: " + ", ".join(sorted(p.name for p in VAULT.iterdir())))
139
140# Read the header back from disk, exactly as a tool does after a reboot.
141header = json.loads((VAULT / "vault.json").read_text())
142# Try a wrong passphrase; the try block catches the failure instead of stopping the program.
143try:
144 # Attempt to unwrap slot 0 with a wrong (but similar) passphrase.
145 unlock(b"LAB-ONLY Maple-Vault 2025!", header["slots"][0])
146 # This line would run only if a wrong passphrase could open the vault; it must never print.
147 print("UNEXPECTED: the wrong passphrase opened the vault")
148# InvalidUnwrap means the integrity check of the wrapped key failed: the KEK was wrong.
149except InvalidUnwrap:
150 # Print the expected result.
151 print("Wrong passphrase -> key unwrap FAILED (InvalidUnwrap): ACCESS REFUSED, as expected")
152
153# Unwrap the DEK from slot 1 with the recovery password read from its offline file.
154dek = unlock(pathlib.Path("RECOVERY-PASSWORD_store-offline.txt").read_text().strip().encode(), header["slots"][1])
155# Rebuild the cipher object with the recovered DEK.
156aead = AESGCM(dek)
157# Print the fingerprint of the recovered DEK: it is the same key as in step 4.
158print(f"Recovery password accepted: DEK fingerprint {fp(dek)} (same key as step 4)")
159# Decrypt each file of the manifest and compare it with the original plaintext.
160for entry in header["files"]:
161 # Read nonce + ciphertext + tag from the vault.
162 blob = (VAULT / entry["file"]).read_bytes()
163 # The original file name (without .nmv) is the AAD that was bound to the ciphertext at encryption time.
164 name = entry["file"][:-4]
165 # Decrypt: AES-GCM first verifies the 16-byte tag, then returns the plaintext.
166 plain = aead.decrypt(blob[:12], blob[12:], name.encode())
167 # Compare the digest of the decrypted bytes with the digest of the original file.
168 same = hashlib.sha256(plain).digest() == hashlib.sha256((SRC / name).read_bytes()).digest()
169 # Print the verdict for this file.
170 print(f" {name:<22} decrypted {len(plain):>6} bytes SHA-256 {'IDENTICAL to the original' if same else 'DIFFERENT'}")
171
172# Read the encrypted ledger into a byte array that can be modified in memory (the file on disk is not changed).
173blob = bytearray((VAULT / "ledger_2026-Q3.csv.nmv").read_bytes())
174# Flip the lowest bit of byte 100 (inside the ciphertext), as a disk fault or an attacker could.
175blob[100] ^= 0x01
176# Try to decrypt the modified copy.
177try:
178 # Decryption checks the authentication tag before it returns any plaintext.
179 aead.decrypt(bytes(blob[:12]), bytes(blob[12:]), b"ledger_2026-Q3.csv")
180 # This line would run only if modified ciphertext were accepted; it must never print.
181 print("UNEXPECTED: modified ciphertext was accepted")
182# InvalidTag means the tag computed over the modified data does not match the stored tag.
183except InvalidTag:
184 # Print the expected result.
185 print("1 bit changed -> authentication tag mismatch (InvalidTag): modified data REJECTED")
186
187# Take the SHA-256 digests of all encrypted files before the change.
188before = [hashlib.sha256((VAULT / e["file"]).read_bytes()).hexdigest() for e in header["files"]]
189# Draw a new random salt for the new passphrase.
190new_salt = os.urandom(16)
191# Re-wrap the same DEK with a KEK derived from the new passphrase, and replace slot 0.
192header["slots"][0] = {"name": "passphrase", "salt": new_salt.hex(), "wrapped_dek": aes_key_wrap(derive_kek(b"LAB-ONLY Maple-Vault 2026-10!", new_salt), dek).hex()}
193# Save the updated header.
194(VAULT / "vault.json").write_text(json.dumps(header, indent=2))
195# Take the digests again after the change.
196after = [hashlib.sha256((VAULT / e["file"]).read_bytes()).hexdigest() for e in header["files"]]
197# Print the comparison: identical digests prove that no data was re-encrypted, only one 40-byte slot changed.
198print(f"New passphrase set: slot 0 rewritten ({len(header['slots'][0]['wrapped_dek']) // 2} bytes); encrypted files {'UNCHANGED' if before == after else 'CHANGED'} ({len(after)} of {len(after)} digests identical)")
199
200# Build a "retired" copy of the header with both key slots removed, as when a disk is decommissioned.
201retired = dict(header, slots=[])
202# Save the retired copy next to the vault, so the working vault stays usable for the validation of Lesson 3.
203(VAULT / "vault_retired.json").write_text(json.dumps(retired, indent=2))
204# Count the slots left in the retired copy: zero slots means no secret can recover the DEK, so the ciphertext is permanently unreadable.
205print(f"Retired header: {len(retired['slots'])} key slots -> no passphrase or recovery password can rebuild the DEK (cryptographic erase, NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2)")
206
207# Print the closing summary of the evidence produced by this run.
208print("SUMMARY: plaintext readable (marker found) -> ciphertext unreadable (marker gone, entropy ~8) -> wrong passphrase refused -> recovery works -> tampering detected -> passphrase change re-wraps the key only -> erase by destroying key slots.")
209
Live visualization — the vault building, slot by slot
Ready. Press ▶ Start to reproduce the recorded run, or Step to advance one step at a time.

  

    
How to run it, and what each step does

    
Run: On a lab VM: python3 -m pip install cryptography, then python3 nm_envelope_vault.py. It writes the folders ClientRecords_demo and ClientRecords_vault and the recovery-password file in the current directory. — Recorded 2026-10-10 11:57 UTC · Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (Linux 6.18.44-fc-v114) · Python 3.13.16 · OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024 · nginx version: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu) · wireguard-go v0.0.20230223 + wireguard-tools v1.0.20210914

    
  1. Step 1 (s1). Load the tools: Python's standard library and the cryptography package.
  2. Step 2 (s2). Create the fictional client-records folder: three files, laboratory data only.
  3. Step 3 (s3). Measure the plaintext: entropy in bits per byte, and whether the marker is visible.
  4. Step 4 (s4). Generate the DEK (Data Encryption Key): 256 random bits that will encrypt every file.
  5. Step 5 (s5). Encrypt every file with AES-256-GCM; the file name is bound to the ciphertext as AAD.
  6. Step 6 (s6). Measure the ciphertext: entropy close to 8 bits per byte, and the marker has disappeared.
  7. Step 7 (s7). Derive the KEK (Key Encryption Key) from the passphrase: PBKDF2, 500,000 rounds, random salt.
  8. Step 8 (s8). Wrap (encrypt) the DEK with the KEK: this is key slot 0 of the vault header.
  9. Step 9 (s9). Create a 48-digit recovery password and wrap the same DEK a second time: key slot 1.
  10. Step 10 (s10). Write the vault header (algorithms, two key slots, file manifest) and lock the vault.
  11. Step 11 (s11). Locked vault: try a wrong passphrase on slot 0 - the unwrap must fail.
  12. Step 12 (s12). Unlock with the recovery password (slot 1), decrypt every file, compare SHA-256 with the originals.
  13. Step 13 (s13). Tamper test: change one bit of an encrypted file - AES-GCM must refuse to decrypt it.
  14. Step 14 (s14). Change the passphrase: only slot 0 is rewritten; the encrypted files stay byte-for-byte identical.
  15. Step 15 (s15). Cryptographic erase demonstration: a header copy without key slots can never unlock the data.
  16. Step 16 (s16). Summary: what this run proved, in the order of the validation checklist.

  

  
  
  

▣Diagrams and figures for this lesson
🂠Flashcards — five per sub-topic
Click a card to reveal the answer on its back.
1.1 — Data at rest, and what encrypting it does
Concept 1
What are the three states of data, and which one is 'data at rest'?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
In transit (moving on a network), in use (in the memory of a running program), and at rest (stored on a medium not being processed). Data at rest is the stored state — disks, files, backups, cloud objects; NIST SP 800-111 is the guide to encrypting data at rest on end-user devices.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What exactly does encryption of stored data protect against?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Someone obtaining the medium while the system is off or locked: a lost or stolen laptop, a pulled disk, a returned machine, a copied backup, a stolen snapshot. The medium that leaves your control is unreadable.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What does encryption at rest NOT protect against?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
A running, unlocked system. The OS decrypts transparently for authorized programs, so a logged-in user or malware running as that user reads the files normally. It is not a substitute for access control.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
Which AES modes are used for disks versus files, and why?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
XTS (NIST SP 800-38E) for whole disks and volumes; an AEAD mode such as GCM (SP 800-38D) for files and messages, because GCM also detects any change to the data.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
Which CIS Safeguards require encryption at rest?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
CIS Safeguard 3.6 (encrypt data on end-user devices) and 3.11 (encrypt sensitive data at rest); 3.9 covers removable media and 3.10 covers data in transit.
◂ click to flip back
1.2 — Where the encryption happens: five layers
Concept 1
Name the five layers where stored data can be encrypted.
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Full disk/volume, encrypted container, file/archive, cloud server-side, and cloud client-side. Mature designs combine more than one.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What is full-disk encryption, and name one tool per OS.
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Encryption of every sector of a drive or partition below the file system. BitLocker (Windows), LUKS2/dm-crypt (Linux), FileVault (macOS).
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What is an encrypted container, and which free tool makes one?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
One large file that mounts as a drive when unlocked and is a single opaque file when locked. VeraCrypt (AES in XTS mode) is the standard free tool; LAB_06 accepts it.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
Why encrypt an empty volume before putting data in it?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Encrypting a disk that already holds plaintext does not immediately erase old plaintext from spare sectors; creating a fresh encrypted container and writing into it avoids leftover readable data.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
Are encryption at rest and in transit alternatives?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
No — they are complementary. A file can be encrypted on the disk (at rest) and travel inside the VPN (in transit); both are needed, each for a different threat.
◂ click to flip back
1.3 — Keys, recovery, and erase
Concept 1
What is envelope encryption?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
A DEK (Data Encryption Key) encrypts the data; one or more KEKs (Key Encryption Keys) wrap the DEK, each wrapped copy kept in a key slot. Used by BitLocker, LUKS2, VeraCrypt and cloud KMS.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
Why can you change a passphrase without re-encrypting the data?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Because the passphrase only protects a KEK that wraps the DEK. Changing it rewrites one small key slot; the data stays encrypted under the same unchanged DEK.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What two properties does PBKDF2 give, with a salt and iterations?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The salt makes the same passphrase produce a different key on each system (defeating precomputed tables); the iteration count sets a fixed cost per guess, slowing brute force.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What is a BitLocker recovery password, and where is it stored?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
A 48-digit number in eight groups of six that unlocks the volume in recovery mode. It is stored separately from the data — printed in a safe or escrowed — never on the same disk.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
What is cryptographic erase?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Destroying every wrapped copy of the DEK (every key slot) so the ciphertext can never be decrypted, without overwriting the medium. NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 lists it as a purge technique.
◂ click to flip back
1.4 — Encryption in cloud storage
Concept 1
What does the cloud shared responsibility model say about encryption?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The provider secures the infrastructure ('of the cloud'); the customer is responsible for configuring protection of their data ('in the cloud'), including encryption choices.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What is the default encryption of new Amazon S3 objects, since when?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Every new object has been encrypted by default since January 5, 2023, with SSE-S3 (AES-256). SSE-KMS can be chosen to control and audit the key.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What changed for S3 SSE-C in April 2026?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
SSE-C (server-side encryption with customer-provided keys) is blocked by default for new general-purpose buckets since April 6, 2026.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
Can Azure Storage encryption be turned off?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
No. Azure Storage encryption is always on with AES-256 and cannot be disabled; keys are Microsoft-managed by default or customer-managed in Azure Key Vault.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
When do you need client-side encryption instead of server-side?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
When the data must be unreadable to the provider itself. Encrypt on the company computer before upload (e.g. Cryptomator, age, GnuPG); server-side alone trusts the provider with the keys.
◂ click to flip back
✎Practice — 4 MCQ and 2 MSQ
Choose your answer(s), use the hint if needed, then reveal the answer and the explanation. MCQ = one answer; MSQ = several answers (the number is shown).



  
MCQone answer

  
1. A NorthMaple laptop with a BitLocker-encrypted disk is stolen while powered off. What does the encryption prevent?

  
The thief reading the client files by removing the disk and reading it in another computer
A logged-in user on the running laptop from opening the files
Malware from encrypting the files for ransom
The laptop from being tracked or located

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Encryption at rest protects the medium when the system is off or locked, not a running session.

  
Encryption at rest makes the stored bytes unreadable to anyone who obtains the medium while it is off or locked — exactly the stolen-disk case. It does nothing against a running, unlocked session (option 2), is unrelated to ransomware encrypting files (3), and has nothing to do with device tracking (4).





  
MCQone answer

  
2. Which NIST mode of AES is designed for encrypting whole disks and volumes?

  
XTS-AES (SP 800-38E)
GCM (SP 800-38D)
PBKDF2 (SP 800-132)
RSA-OAEP

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. One mode is for storage devices; the other is an authenticated mode for messages and files.

  
XTS-AES (SP 800-38E) is the mode for storage devices and is used by BitLocker, LUKS2 and VeraCrypt. GCM (SP 800-38D) is an AEAD mode for files and messages. PBKDF2 is a key-derivation function, not a cipher mode, and RSA-OAEP is a public-key scheme, not a disk mode.





  
MCQone answer

  
3. In envelope encryption, why can a passphrase be changed without re-encrypting any data?

  
The passphrase protects a KEK that wraps the DEK, so only the small key slot is rewritten
The data is not really encrypted until the first change
Changing the passphrase re-encrypts everything instantly in the background
The passphrase is the key that directly encrypts the data

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Think about which key actually touches the data, and which key only wraps another key.

  
The DEK encrypts the data and never changes; the passphrase only derives a KEK that wraps the DEK into a key slot. Changing the passphrase rewrites one ~40-byte slot, not the data (ruling out options 2–4, and option 4 describes the opposite of envelope encryption).





  
MCQone answer

  
4. Since April 6, 2026, which Amazon S3 option is blocked by default for new general-purpose buckets?

  
SSE-C (customer-provided keys)
SSE-S3 (S3-managed keys)
SSE-KMS (AWS KMS keys)
Default encryption of new objects

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. The blocked option is the one where the customer sends their own key with each request.

  
AWS blocks SSE-C (server-side encryption with customer-provided keys) by default for new general-purpose buckets since April 6, 2026. SSE-S3 remains the default, SSE-KMS remains available, and default encryption of new objects has been on since January 5, 2023.





  
MSQ (Select 3)Select 3

  
5. Which statements about keys and recovery for stored data are correct? (Select 3)

  
A recovery secret must be stored separately from the data it can unlock
PBKDF2's salt makes the same passphrase produce a different key on each system
Cryptographic erase destroys every wrapped copy of the DEK so the ciphertext can't be decrypted
A higher PBKDF2 iteration count makes each guess cheaper for an attacker
A recovery key stored in the same folder as the container is good practice
The DEK should be printed and taped to the laptop for convenience

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Three are sound key-management practice; three describe mistakes or the opposite of the truth.

  
Correct: a recovery secret is kept apart from the data (1); the salt diversifies the derived key per system (2); cryptographic erase destroys the key slots (3). Wrong: a higher iteration count makes each guess MORE expensive, not cheaper (4); storing the recovery key beside the container (5) or taping the DEK to the laptop (6) cancels the encryption.





  
MSQ (Select 3)Select 3

  
6. Which statements about where and how stored data is encrypted are correct? (Select 3)

  
Full-disk encryption covers every sector of a drive below the file system
An encrypted container is one file that mounts as a drive when unlocked
Encryption at rest and in transit are complementary, not alternatives
A running, unlocked system keeps all files encrypted to the logged-in user
Server-side cloud encryption makes data unreadable to the provider itself
Encrypting a disk already full of plaintext instantly erases the old plaintext

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Two of the false options describe a protection that encryption at rest does not actually provide.

  
Correct: full-disk encryption works below the file system (1); a container mounts as a drive when unlocked (2); at-rest and in-transit encryption are complementary (3). Wrong: a logged-in user reads files decrypted (4); server-side encryption does NOT hide data from the provider — that needs client-side encryption (5); encrypting a used disk does not instantly erase old plaintext from spare sectors (6).


↑ Back to top
2.1Why an internal service needs HTTPS too
Slide 17
Key terms
HTTP vs HTTPS — Over HTTP the page, login and cookie travel as plaintext; HTTPS carries HTTP inside TLS.
What TLS does — Encrypts the traffic, authenticates the server, and detects tampering.
TLS versions — TLS 1.3 (RFC 9846) is current; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996) and must be refused.
Certificate — Binds a server name to a public key; the client checks it is signed by a trusted authority and that the typed name is listed.
Zoning is not confidentiality — The perimeter limits who reaches a segment; one compromised host inside is enough, so internal services need HTTPS too (CIS 3.10).
2.2The certificate: self-signed, with the right names
Slide 18 Slide 19 Slide 20
Key terms
Self-signed certificate — A certificate that is its own issuer (Subject = Issuer); trusted only after it is installed or its fingerprint checked.
No public CA for internal names — Public CAs may not issue for internal names; Let's Encrypt certifies only publicly resolvable names.
Subject Alternative Name (SAN) — The field browsers check for the host name; the Common Name is ignored (RFC 9525). A wrong SAN causes a name-mismatch error.
CA:FALSE / serverAuth — Basic Constraints CA:FALSE forbids signing other certificates; Extended Key Usage serverAuth marks it valid to authenticate a server.
Validity — 200 days maximum for public certificates since March 15, 2026 (100 days in 2027, 47 in 2029); OpenSSL's own default is only 30 days.
2.3Serving HTTPS only, and protecting the key
Slide 21 Slide 22
Key terms
HTTPS-only — Port 80 returns 301 to https:// and serves no page; port 443 serves the page over TLS 1.2/1.3.
HSTS — HTTP Strict Transport Security (RFC 6797): a header telling a browser that once trusted to refuse plain HTTP.
Private-key protection — The key is root-only, mode 600, generated on the server and never copied to clients; the certificate is public (644).
openssl s_client — Opens a TLS session and reports the version, cipher suite and certificate; recorded run negotiated TLS 1.3, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384.
Server options — nginx (ssl_certificate, ssl_certificate_key, ssl_protocols), Apache mod_ssl, or an IIS HTTPS binding.
2.4Distributing trust and registering the certificate
Slide 23 Slide 24
Key terms
Trust warning — An untrusted client refuses a self-signed certificate — correctly; the fix is to install it, not to click past the warning.
Fingerprint check — Confirm the certificate by comparing its SHA-256 fingerprint out of band before installing it.
Distribute the public certificate — Only the public .cer (DER form) is imported into the client trust store; the private key never leaves the server.
Device registry — Records service, host, port, fingerprint, expiry and a renewal date 30 days earlier.
Expiry — An expired certificate breaks the service like a wrong one; registration with a renewal date keeps it maintainable.

◎Real-life example
Slide 25
Task
Move NorthMaple's internal intranet from plain HTTP to HTTPS only, with a self-signed certificate the workstations trust after a fingerprint check.
▸ Feeds a future lab: LAB_06 Part 2, HTTPS deliverable (Chapter 6 of the Final Project and of the Course Procedure Manual; device registry in Chapter 5).
How it relates to this lecture. This is the HTTPS part of LAB_06 Part 2 ("enable HTTPS with a self-signed certificate on one internal service"). The certificate, the HTTPS-only configuration and the device-registry line become section 6.3 (Procedure) of the Course Procedure Manual and a row of the Chapter 5 device registry; Lesson 3 then validates that the service answers only over HTTPS.
NorthMaple's intranet page, which indexes client files, runs on an internal host (the Servers-zone address 192.168.20.10 in the VM plan — NM-FS01 on the Windows path, a Linux service host on the Linux path) over plain HTTP. Today you create a self-signed ECDSA (ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm), Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) P-256 key and certificate whose SAN lists both the name and the address, configure the service so port 80 only redirects and port 443 serves the page over TLS 1.2/1.3 with HSTS, protect the private key as root-only mode 600, export the public certificate for the workstations, verify it with openssl s_client, and record the registry line. The recorded run produced exactly this: a 301 on port 80, a TLS 1.3 session on port 443, and a refusal for any client that does not yet trust the certificate.
DeliverableThe self-signed certificate (public .crt/.cer), the HTTPS-only service configuration, the private-key permissions, and the device-registry line — the HTTPS evidence for Chapter 6 and the registry row for Chapter 5.
Where it goesLAB_06 Part 2, HTTPS deliverable (Chapter 6 of the Final Project and of the Course Procedure Manual; device registry in Chapter 5).

nm_https_enable.shBash with OpenSSL, nginx and curl (Linux path)

  
What it does. Generate the self-signed key and certificate with the right SAN and extensions, configure nginx for HTTPS only with a redirect on port 80, protect the private key, and run five tests that prove the result (plain HTTP redirects, untrusted client refused, trusted client gets 200 + HSTS, TLS 1.3 negotiated, loaded config shows TLS 1.2/1.3 only). Link with the lecture. It performs the real-life example and illustrates every term of sub-topics 2.2 to 2.4: self-signed certificate, SAN, CA:FALSE, serverAuth, private-key permissions, 301 redirect, HSTS, fingerprint and the registry line. The recorded output is reproduced step by step in the HTML player.

  

    
    
    
    
    
    
    ready
  

  

    
1#!/usr/bin/env bash
2# nm_https_enable.sh - Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB), Class 17, Lesson 2 example (Linux path, nginx).
3# TASK: move NorthMaple Accounting Inc.'s internal intranet page from plain HTTP to HTTPS-only
4# with a self-signed certificate, then test the result the way a client computer will see it.
5# LAB ONLY: run it as root inside your own isolated laboratory VM (Legal Notice v1.0, section 3).
6# Requirements: Ubuntu or Debian with nginx, openssl and curl (apt install nginx openssl curl).
7# Usage: sudo bash nm_https_enable.sh
8 
9# Stop at the first failing command (-e), treat an unset variable as an error (-u), and fail a pipeline when any part of it fails (pipefail).
10set -euo pipefail
11# The name users type in the browser; it must appear in the certificate's SAN (Subject Alternative Name).
12SVC_NAME="intranet.northmaple.internal"
13# The Servers-zone address of the internal service (VM plan: 192.168.20.0/24); the certificate lists it too.
14SVC_IP="192.168.20.10"
15# The folder that holds the certificate (public) and, in its private/ sub-folder, the key (secret).
16CERT_DIR="/etc/ssl/northmaple"
17# The private key file: whoever holds it can impersonate the service, so only root may read it.
18KEY="$CERT_DIR/private/intranet.key"
19# The certificate in PEM (Privacy-Enhanced Mail) text format, the file nginx reads.
20CRT="$CERT_DIR/intranet.crt"
21# The same certificate in DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) binary format, the copy handed to client computers.
22CER="$CERT_DIR/intranet.cer"
23# Validity in days: 200, the maximum for public certificates since March 15, 2026; the self-signed certificate keeps the same habit.
24DAYS=200
25# Print the settings, so that the run documents itself.
26echo "Service $SVC_NAME ($SVC_IP); certificate valid $DAYS days; key file $KEY"
27 
28# Create the certificate folder and its private sub-folder (no error if they already exist).
29mkdir -p "$CERT_DIR/private"
30# Mode 700 on the private folder: the owner (root) may read, write and enter it; nobody else may.
31chmod 700 "$CERT_DIR/private"
32# Show the permissions, owner and group of both folders.
33stat -c '%A %U:%G %n' "$CERT_DIR" "$CERT_DIR/private"
34 
35# One command creates an ECDSA P-256 key and a self-signed X.509 certificate: -x509 writes a certificate instead of a request, -noenc stores the key without a passphrase so nginx can start unattended, -days sets the validity (the default is only 30 days), and each -addext adds an extension: the SAN with the name and the address, "not a CA", signature-only key usage, and the serverAuth purpose.
36openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -noenc -keyout "$KEY" -out "$CRT" -days "$DAYS" -sha256 -subj "/O=NorthMaple Accounting Inc. (LAB)/CN=$SVC_NAME" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:$SVC_NAME,IP:$SVC_IP" -addext "basicConstraints=critical,CA:FALSE" -addext "keyUsage=critical,digitalSignature" -addext "extendedKeyUsage=serverAuth" 2>&1
37# Confirm that both files now exist.
38ls -l "$KEY" "$CRT"
39 
40# Make root the owner of the key and of the certificate.
41chown root:root "$KEY" "$CRT"
42# Mode 600 on the key: only root can read or write it.
43chmod 600 "$KEY"
44# Mode 644 on the certificate: everyone may read it, because a certificate contains only public information.
45chmod 644 "$CRT"
46# Show the numeric mode, owner and group of both files.
47stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' "$KEY" "$CRT"
48 
49# Print the fields that matter for an internal HTTPS service, without the long encoded blocks (-noout).
50openssl x509 -in "$CRT" -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName,basicConstraints,keyUsage,extendedKeyUsage
51 
52# -checkhost and -checkip compare a name and an IP address with the SAN and report whether each one matches.
53openssl x509 -in "$CRT" -noout -checkhost "$SVC_NAME" -checkip "$SVC_IP"
54 
55# Print the SHA-256 fingerprint; always ask for -sha256, because without it OpenSSL prints a SHA-1 fingerprint.
56openssl x509 -in "$CRT" -noout -fingerprint -sha256
57# Write the certificate in DER format (.cer): this public file is what NM-WS01 imports; the key never leaves this server.
58openssl x509 -in "$CRT" -outform DER -out "$CER"
59# Show the size of the exported file.
60stat -c '%s bytes %n' "$CER"
61 
62# Create the web root of the intranet.
63mkdir -p /var/www/intranet
64# Write the page: a title and one line of fictional text, nothing real.
65printf '<!doctype html><title>NorthMaple intranet (LAB)</title><h1>NorthMaple intranet</h1><p>Client file index - laboratory page, fictional data.</p>\n' > /var/www/intranet/index.html
66# Show the size of the page.
67stat -c '%s bytes %n' /var/www/intranet/index.html
68 
69# Write the site file; the backslashes keep nginx's own variables ($host, $request_uri) away from the shell.
70cat > /etc/nginx/sites-available/intranet <<EOF
71# Port 80 server: it never serves the page; it only sends browsers to the HTTPS address.
72server {
73    # Listen for plain HTTP on TCP port 80.
74    listen 80;
75    # Answer for the intranet name.
76    server_name $SVC_NAME;
77    # Reply 301 (moved permanently) with the same host and path over HTTPS.
78    return 301 https://\$host\$request_uri;
79# End of the port 80 server.
80}
81# Port 443 server: the only place where the page is served.
82server {
83    # Listen on TCP port 443 with TLS (Transport Layer Security) enabled.
84    listen 443 ssl;
85    # Answer for the intranet name (clients also send it in the TLS SNI field).
86    server_name $SVC_NAME;
87    # The certificate presented to clients.
88    ssl_certificate $CRT;
89    # The private key that proves the server owns that certificate.
90    ssl_certificate_key $KEY;
91    # Accept only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996).
92    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
93    # HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security): a browser that trusts the certificate will refuse plain HTTP for one day (lab value; production uses up to two years).
94    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=86400" always;
95    # The folder that holds the intranet page.
96    root /var/www/intranet;
97    # The file served when the browser asks for the folder itself.
98    index index.html;
99# End of the port 443 server.
100}
101EOF
102# Show the active (non-comment) lines of the new site file.
103grep -v '^\s*#' /etc/nginx/sites-available/intranet
104 
105# Link the site into sites-enabled, the folder nginx actually loads.
106ln -sf /etc/nginx/sites-available/intranet /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/intranet
107# Remove nginx's default welcome site: an unused service is attack surface (hardening, Class 5).
108rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default
109# Test the configuration syntax before applying it: a broken file must never reach the running server.
110nginx -t 2>&1
111# Reload nginx when it is already running, otherwise start it.
112if pgrep -x nginx >/dev/null; then nginx -s reload; else nginx; fi
113# Wait one second, so that the new configuration is active before the tests.
114sleep 1
115 
116# Ask for the page over HTTP (port 80); --resolve maps the name to the address without DNS (Domain Name System); -w prints the status code and the redirect target.
117curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code} -> %{redirect_url}\n" --resolve "$SVC_NAME:80:$SVC_IP" "http://$SVC_NAME/"
118 
119# Ask for the page over HTTPS with the system trust store only; the self-signed certificate is unknown there, so curl stops with exit code 60.
120curl -sS -o /dev/null --resolve "$SVC_NAME:443:$SVC_IP" "https://$SVC_NAME/" 2>&1 || echo "EXPECTED: refused until the certificate is trusted on the client"
121 
122# Use the certificate itself as the trust anchor (--cacert), print the response headers (-D -), discard the page, and keep the two lines that matter.
123curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null --cacert "$CRT" --resolve "$SVC_NAME:443:$SVC_IP" "https://$SVC_NAME/" | grep -i -E '^HTTP|^strict-transport'
124 
125# Open a TLS session with the name in SNI (-servername), trust only our certificate (-CAfile), stop on any verification error, and print a short summary (-brief).
126openssl s_client -connect "$SVC_IP:443" -servername "$SVC_NAME" -CAfile "$CRT" -verify_return_error -brief </dev/null 2>&1 | head -n 9
127 
128# Dump the complete loaded configuration (-T), keep the file names and the ssl_protocols lines, and show each line with the file it comes from; the line in our site overrides the distribution's default for this server.
129nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^# configuration file|ssl_protocols' | grep -B1 ssl_protocols
130 
131# Read the expiry date (notAfter) from the certificate.
132END=$(openssl x509 -in "$CRT" -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2)
133# Read the SHA-256 fingerprint and keep only the hexadecimal value.
134FPR=$(openssl x509 -in "$CRT" -noout -fingerprint -sha256 | cut -d= -f2)
135# Compute the renewal date: 30 days before expiry, so that the replacement is ready in time.
136RENEW=$(date -u -d "$END - 30 days" +%Y-%m-%d)
137# Write the CSV header and the registry line to a file (Final Project, Chapter 5 device registry) and show them on screen.
138printf 'service,host,ip,port,certificate,expires,renew_by,sha256_fingerprint,key_location\nintranet,%s,%s,443,self-signed ECDSA P-256,%s,%s,%s,%s (root only; mode 600)\n' "$SVC_NAME" "$SVC_IP" "$(date -u -d "$END" +%Y-%m-%d)" "$RENEW" "$FPR" "$KEY" | tee "$CERT_DIR/registry_intranet.csv"
139

How to run it, and what each step does

    
Run: As root on a lab VM with nginx installed: sudo bash nm_https_enable.sh. On Windows/IIS the equivalent uses New-SelfSignedCertificate and an HTTPS binding (shown in the links). The host name is resolved locally with curl --resolve, so no DNS server is needed. — Recorded 2026-10-10 11:57 UTC · Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (Linux 6.18.44-fc-v114) · Python 3.13.16 · OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024 · nginx version: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu) · wireguard-go v0.0.20230223 + wireguard-tools v1.0.20210914

    
  1. Step 1 (h1). Settings: service name and address, certificate files, validity, strict error handling.
  2. Step 2 (h2). Create the certificate folders; the private folder is reachable by root only.
  3. Step 3 (h3). Generate the key pair and the self-signed certificate in one OpenSSL command (ECDSA P-256, SAN, serverAuth).
  4. Step 4 (h4). Protect the private key: owner root, mode 600; the certificate stays readable by all (it is public).
  5. Step 5 (h5). Read the certificate: subject, issuer (identical, because it is self-signed), validity dates, extensions.
  6. Step 6 (h6). Check that the name and the address users will type are both covered by the certificate.
  7. Step 7 (h7). Compute the SHA-256 fingerprint for the device registry and export the public DER copy for client computers.
  8. Step 8 (h8). Write the intranet page: a minimal laboratory page with fictional content.
  9. Step 9 (h9). Write the nginx site: port 80 only redirects; port 443 serves the page with TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 only.
  10. Step 10 (h10). Enable the site, remove the default site, test the configuration, then start or reload nginx.
  11. Step 11 (h11). Test 1 - plain HTTP: the service must answer with a redirect, never with the page.
  12. Step 12 (h12). Test 2 - HTTPS from a client that does not trust the certificate yet: the connection must be refused.
  13. Step 13 (h13). Test 3 - HTTPS from a client that trusts the certificate: status 200 and the HSTS header.
  14. Step 14 (h14). Test 4 - TLS details with openssl s_client: protocol version, cipher suite, certificate verification.
  15. Step 15 (h15). Test 5 - read the configuration nginx has loaded: which TLS versions this site accepts.
  16. Step 16 (h16). Write the device-registry line: service, address, fingerprint, expiry date and renewal date.

  

  
  
  

▣Diagrams and figures for this lesson
🂠Flashcards — five per sub-topic
Click a card to reveal the answer on its back.
2.1 — Why an internal service needs HTTPS too
Concept 1
Why does an internal service need HTTPS, not just HTTP?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Over HTTP the page, login, cookie and clicks travel as plaintext; anyone on a segment in between (or the IDS) reads them. Network zoning is not confidentiality (CIS 3.10).
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What three things does TLS do at once?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Encrypts the traffic, authenticates the server (the client knows it is the real service), and detects tampering (altered bytes are rejected).
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What is the current TLS version, and which are deprecated?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
TLS 1.3 (RFC 9846, which replaced RFC 8446 in 2026). TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996 and must be refused.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What does a certificate bind, and what does the client check?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
It binds a server name to a public key. The client checks that the certificate is signed by a trusted authority and that the typed name is listed in the certificate.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
Why is TLS encryption worthless without the certificate check?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Because an attacker could present their own key and encrypt the channel to themselves. The certificate ties the encrypted channel to the right, verified server.
◂ click to flip back
2.2 — The certificate: self-signed, with the right names
Concept 1
Why can't an internal name get a public CA certificate?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements forbid public CAs from issuing for internal names, and Let's Encrypt only certifies publicly resolvable names. Use a private CA or a self-signed certificate.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What makes a certificate 'self-signed'?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Its Subject and Issuer are identical — it signs for itself, with no third party vouching for it — so clients trust it only after it is installed or its fingerprint is checked.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
Which certificate field do modern browsers check for the host name?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The Subject Alternative Name (SAN) only. Since 2017 Chrome and other browsers ignore the Common Name (CN); a missing or wrong SAN causes a name-mismatch error (RFC 9525).
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What do CA:FALSE and EKU serverAuth mean on a server certificate?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
CA:FALSE (Basic Constraints, critical) means it may not sign other certificates; serverAuth (Extended Key Usage) means it is valid to authenticate a server, not to sign e-mail or code.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
What is the maximum validity of a public TLS certificate now, and next?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
200 days since March 15, 2026; it drops to 100 days in 2027 and 47 days in 2029 (CA/Browser Forum). Internal certificates aren't bound by this but the habit is kept.
◂ click to flip back
2.3 — Serving HTTPS only, and protecting the key
Concept 1
When is 'enabling HTTPS' actually finished?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
When port 80 no longer serves the page — it returns 301 to the https:// address and nothing else — and port 443 serves the page over TLS 1.2/1.3.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
Which TLS versions should the service accept, and what is HSTS?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 (ssl_protocols). HSTS (RFC 6797) is a header telling a browser that once trusted the certificate to refuse plain HTTP afterwards.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
How is the private key protected in the recorded run?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
It lives in a root-only directory (700), the key file is mode 600 (owner read/write only), the certificate is 644 (public). The key is generated on the server and never leaves it.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What do you copy to clients — the key or the certificate?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Only the public certificate (.cer). The private key never leaves the server; whoever holds it can impersonate the service.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
What did the recorded TLS session negotiate?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
TLS 1.3 with the cipher suite TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 — the same AES-GCM used for files in Lesson 1, now protecting data in transit.
◂ click to flip back
2.4 — Distributing trust and registering the certificate
Concept 1
Why does an untrusted client refuse a self-signed certificate, and what is the fix?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Because it chains to no authority the client knows — the warning is correct. The fix is to install the certificate as trusted on each workstation after confirming it, not to click past the warning.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
How do you confirm a certificate is the right one before trusting it?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Compare its SHA-256 fingerprint out of band — read over the phone or carried on a USB key — before installing it. The recorded fingerprint begins 6E:46:B6:E3…
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What is distributed to clients, and in what form?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Only the public certificate, exported as a .cer file in DER form, imported into the Trusted Root store (Windows) or system trust anchors (Linux).
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What is recorded in the device registry for a certificate?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The service, host and port, the SHA-256 fingerprint, the expiry date, and a renewal date 30 days earlier, so the replacement is ready before it expires.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
Why does an expired certificate matter as much as a wrong one?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
An expired certificate breaks the service exactly as a wrong one does. Registering it with a renewal date turns a one-time setup into a maintainable control.
◂ click to flip back
✎Practice — 4 MCQ and 2 MSQ
Choose your answer(s), use the hint if needed, then reveal the answer and the explanation. MCQ = one answer; MSQ = several answers (the number is shown).



  
MCQone answer

  
1. A browser shows a name-mismatch error for the intranet certificate even though the Common Name is correct. What is the most likely cause?

  
The host name is not listed in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN)
The certificate uses AES-256 instead of AES-128
The private key is stored with mode 600
The certificate is valid for 200 days instead of 100

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Modern browsers check one specific field for the host name and ignore another.

  
Since 2017 browsers check the host name against the SAN only and ignore the Common Name (RFC 9525), so a missing or wrong SAN causes a name mismatch regardless of the CN. The cipher strength (2), the correct key permissions (3) and the validity period (4) do not cause a name-mismatch error.





  
MCQone answer

  
2. What is the correct behaviour of the service on TCP port 80 after HTTPS is enabled?

  
Return 301 Moved Permanently to the https:// address and serve no page
Serve the page normally as a fallback for old browsers
Serve the login form but not the rest of the site
Close silently with no response at all is the only acceptable option

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. The page, the login and the cookie must never be sent in clear.

  
Port 80 should return 301 to the https:// address and serve nothing else, so no content ever travels in clear. Serving any page or form on port 80 (options 2–3) leaks plaintext. Closing the port is acceptable too, but it is not the ONLY acceptable option, so option 4's wording is wrong.





  
MCQone answer

  
3. Why can NorthMaple's internal name intranet.northmaple.internal not receive a Let's Encrypt certificate?

  
Public CAs may not issue certificates for internal, non-public names
Let's Encrypt only issues certificates for ECDSA keys
Internal names require a 47-day certificate that Let's Encrypt cannot make
Self-signed certificates are illegal under the CA/Browser Forum rules

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. The limit is about who can prove ownership of the name on the public Internet.

  
Public CAs, including Let's Encrypt, cannot issue for internal names that are not publicly resolvable (CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements). It is unrelated to key type (2); the 47-day limit is a 2029 change for public certificates, not an internal-name rule (3); and self-signed certificates are perfectly legal (4).





  
MCQone answer

  
4. Before installing the self-signed certificate on a workstation, how do you confirm it is the right one?

  
Compare its SHA-256 fingerprint out of band with the server's
Check that the browser shows a green padlock
Confirm the file size matches 592 bytes
Trust it because it came from the internal network

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. You need a check that an attacker substituting a different certificate could not fake.

  
The SHA-256 fingerprint, compared out of band (phone or USB), uniquely identifies the certificate and cannot be faked by a substitute. A padlock only appears after trust is already granted (2); file size is not an identity (3); and 'it came from inside' is exactly the assumption an attacker on the segment would exploit (4).





  
MSQ (Select 3)Select 3

  
5. Which fields or settings make the intranet certificate correct for a server? (Select 3)

  
subjectAltName listing the name and the IP address
Basic Constraints CA:FALSE (critical)
Extended Key Usage serverAuth
Basic Constraints CA:TRUE so it can sign other certificates
Extended Key Usage codeSigning
Key Usage keyCertSign so the server can issue certificates

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. A server certificate authenticates a server and must never be able to sign other certificates.

  
Correct: the SAN with name and IP (1); CA:FALSE so it cannot sign other certificates (2); serverAuth so it authenticates a server (3). Wrong: CA:TRUE (4) and keyCertSign (6) would let it act as a CA, which a server certificate must not; codeSigning (5) is the wrong purpose entirely.





  
MSQ (Select 4)Select 4

  
6. Which practices correctly protect and manage the service's private key and certificate? (Select 4)

  
Store the private key as root-only, mode 600
Generate the key on the server and never copy it to clients
Distribute only the public certificate (.cer) to workstations
Register the certificate with a renewal date before it expires
Email the private key to each workstation so clients can verify it
Set the certificate file to mode 600 so nobody can read it

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. The key is the secret; the certificate is public. Two options confuse the two.

  
Correct: key is root-only mode 600 (1), generated on the server and never copied (2); only the public certificate is distributed (3); and it is registered with a renewal date (4). Wrong: emailing the private key (5) hands over the ability to impersonate the service; the certificate is public and should be world-readable (644), not 600 (6).


↑ Back to top
3.1Why validation is a step of its own
Slide 28 Slide 29
Key terms
Validation — Confirming with a repeatable test that a control works, and keeping the result for a second person to check.
Four parts — Expected (written first from the design), test, observed (recorded exactly), evidence (kept, named, dated).
Positive control — The same test where the answer must be 'yes' (marker found in plaintext); proves the test works.
Negative test — Trying what must fail and recording the failure (wrong passphrase refused); an expected failure is a pass.
Claim vs evidence — A checkbox, padlock or 'connected' is a claim; validation turns it into evidence.
3.2Validating data at rest
Slide 30
Key terms
Marker test — A unique string placed in plaintext and searched for: found in plaintext (control), absent from ciphertext.
Entropy — Average information per byte; encrypted data scores near 8.0, text about 4.6–4.8. Supports but does not prove encryption.
Manual key test — Wrong passphrase refused, right one opens and matches — the strongest data-at-rest evidence (a screenshot).
Recorded result — Marker found in 3/3 plaintext, 0/3 ciphertext; ciphertext entropy ≈ 7.99.
Why a control — Compressed data also scores high, so entropy is used alongside the marker test, never alone.
3.3Validating HTTPS
Slide 31
Key terms
HTTP redirect test — Request over HTTP and confirm a 301 redirect, never the page (negative test).
Fingerprint match — The certificate the server presents must match the registry line byte for byte (SHA-256).
Host-name check — The TLS library accepts the certificate only because the name is in the SAN — set in Lesson 2.
Recorded result — TLS 1.3, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, fingerprint matched, host name verified, HSTS present.
Deeper tools — testssl.sh and nmap ssl-enum-ciphers list every protocol and cipher accepted, to confirm TLS 1.0/1.1 are refused.
3.4Validating the tunnel
Slide 32 Slide 33
Key terms
Two-point capture — Capture on the firewall WAN (encrypted) and on wg0 (after decryption) and compare.
Canary — A unique string sent through the tunnel; absent on the WAN, present on wg0 (positive control).
Recorded WAN — 34 WireGuard messages and nothing else; canary and service name not found; entropy ≈ 7.97.
wg show — Prints the latest handshake and bytes transferred per peer; never prints a private key.
Capture menus — pfSense: Diagnostics > Packet Capture. OPNsense: Interfaces > Diagnostics > Packet capture.

What it does. Run every validation of LAB_06 Part 2 in one pass — data at rest (marker, entropy, manual key test), HTTPS (redirect, TLS version, fingerprint vs registry, host name, HSTS), and the tunnel (read the two capture files for WireGuard-only, canary absent on WAN and present on wg0, plus wg show) — and write a dated evidence table.
