1#!/usr/bin/env python3
2# nm_validate_encryption.py - Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB), Class 17, Lesson 3 example.
3# TASK: collect the LAB_06 validation evidence in one run - the stored data cannot be read
4# without its key, the intranet answers only over HTTPS, and the VPN (Virtual Private Network)
5# traffic is encrypted on the untrusted network - and write it as an evidence table for
6# section 6.4 (Validation) of the Course Procedure Manual.
7# LAB ONLY: run it only against your own laboratory systems and your own captures
8# (Legal Notice v1.0, sections 3 and 4). Requirements: Python 3.10 or newer, standard library only.
9# Usage: python3 nm_validate_encryption.py   (adapt the settings of step v1 to your laboratory)
10 
11# Import the standard-library modules: socket and ssl open network and TLS (Transport Layer Security) connections, hashlib computes digests, math computes entropy, struct reads binary packet headers, csv reads and writes tables, pathlib reads files, datetime stamps each result.
12import socket, ssl, hashlib, math, struct, csv, pathlib, datetime
13# The name and the Servers-zone address of the intranet (Lesson 2).
14SVC_NAME, SVC_IP = "intranet.northmaple.internal", "192.168.20.10"
15# The certificate exported in Lesson 2 (the trust anchor of this client) and the registry file that holds its recorded fingerprint.
16CAFILE, REGISTRY_CSV = "intranet.crt", "registry_intranet.csv"
17# The two captures taken on NM-FW01 during the test: its WAN (Wide Area Network) interface, and its tunnel interface wg0, where packets are already decrypted.
18WAN_PCAP, TUNNEL_PCAP = "wan_capture.pcap", "tunnel_wg0.pcap"
19# The canary: a unique string sent inside the tunnel during the capture; it must be visible inside the tunnel and invisible on the WAN.
20CANARY = b"NM-CANARY-1710"
21# The output of "wg show" saved on NM-FW01 during the same test.
22WG_SHOW = "wg_show_fw01.txt"
23# The Lesson 1 folders (plaintext copy and encrypted vault) and the marker written at the top of every plaintext record.
24PLAIN, VAULT, MARKER = pathlib.Path("ClientRecords_demo"), pathlib.Path("ClientRecords_vault"), b"NORTHMAPLE-CONFIDENTIAL"
25# The evidence table: one row per test.
26EVIDENCE = []
27# Define the function that records one test: identifier, what was checked, expected result, observed result, verdict (True = PASS, False = FAIL, None = MANUAL), and where the evidence comes from.
28def record(test_id, check, expected, observed, ok, source):
29    # Translate the verdict into the word written in the table.
30    verdict = "MANUAL" if ok is None else ("PASS" if ok else "FAIL")
31    # Add the row, stamped with the current UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) time.
32    EVIDENCE.append({"test": test_id, "check": check, "expected": expected, "observed": observed, "result": verdict, "source": source, "checked_at_utc": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")})
33    # Print the row on screen as it is recorded.
34    print(f"  {test_id:<3} {verdict:<6} {check}: {observed}")
35# Define the Shannon entropy in bits per byte (8.0 = all byte values equally frequent).
36def entropy(data):
37    # Count each of the 256 byte values.
38    counts = [0] * 256
39    # Add one to the counter of every byte met.
40    for b in data: counts[b] += 1
41    # Shannon's formula: the sum of -p x log2(p) over the byte values present.
42    return -sum(c / len(data) * math.log2(c / len(data)) for c in counts if c)
43# Define a reader for classic pcap files (the format "tcpdump -w" writes); it returns the IPv4 packets of the capture.
44def packets(path):
45    # Read the whole capture into memory.
46    raw = pathlib.Path(path).read_bytes()
47    # The first 4 bytes give the byte order: d4 c3 b2 a1 on disk means little-endian numbers.
48    endian = "<" if raw[:4] == b"\xd4\xc3\xb2\xa1" else ">"
49    # Bytes 20 to 23 give the link type: 1 = Ethernet frames, 101 = raw IP (a tunnel interface such as wg0).
50    linktype = struct.unpack(endian + "I", raw[20:24])[0]
51    # The list of IPv4 packets found, and the position of the first record (after the 24-byte global header).
52    found, pos = [], 24
53    # Read one record at a time until the end of the file.
54    while pos + 16 <= len(raw):
55        # Each 16-byte record header holds the timestamp (seconds, microseconds), the captured length and the original length.
56        sec, usec, caplen, _ = struct.unpack(endian + "IIII", raw[pos:pos + 16])
57        # Take the frame bytes that follow the record header.
58        frame = raw[pos + 16:pos + 16 + caplen]
59        # Move the position to the next record.
60        pos += 16 + caplen
61        # Remove the 14-byte Ethernet header when the interface is an Ethernet-type interface.
62        ip = frame[14:] if linktype == 1 else frame
63        # Keep IPv4 packets only (the first half-byte of an IPv4 header is 4).
64        if ip and ip[0] >> 4 == 4: found.append(ip)
65    # Return the IPv4 packets in capture order.
66    return found
67# Define a function that splits an IPv4 packet into protocol number, ports and payload.
68def dissect(ip):
69    # The IP header length is the low half-byte of the first byte, counted in 4-byte words.
70    ihl = (ip[0] & 15) * 4
71    # Byte 9 is the protocol number: 6 = TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), 17 = UDP (User Datagram Protocol).
72    proto = ip[9]
73    # For anything other than TCP or UDP (for example ICMP, the ping protocol), return the bytes after the IP header.
74    if proto not in (6, 17): return proto, 0, 0, ip[ihl:]
75    # The first 4 bytes of a TCP or UDP header are the source and destination ports.
76    sport, dport = struct.unpack("!HH", ip[ihl:ihl + 4])
77    # A UDP header is 8 bytes long; a TCP header states its own length in the high half-byte of its 13th byte.
78    off = 8 if proto == 17 else (ip[ihl + 12] >> 4) * 4
79    # Return the protocol, both ports, and the payload that follows the transport header.
80    return proto, sport, dport, ip[ihl + off:]
81# Announce the start of the validation.
82print(f"Validating LAB_06 Part 2 for {SVC_NAME} ({SVC_IP}) - evidence table: C17_validation_evidence.csv")
83 
84# List the plaintext files of the Lesson 1 source folder.
85plain = sorted(PLAIN.glob("*"))
86# Keep the files in which the marker is found.
87hits = [p.name for p in plain if MARKER in p.read_bytes()]
88# Record the result: a marker test that cannot find the marker in plaintext would prove nothing about the ciphertext.
89record("D1", "Marker test detects plaintext (positive control)", f"marker found in {len(plain)} of {len(plain)} files", f"marker found in {len(hits)} of {len(plain)} files", len(hits) == len(plain) > 0, str(PLAIN))
90 
91# List the encrypted files of the vault.
92enc = sorted(VAULT.glob("*.nmv"))
93# Keep the encrypted files that still contain the marker (expected: none).
94leaks = [p.name for p in enc if MARKER in p.read_bytes()]
95# Record the marker result.
96record("D2", "Marker absent from every encrypted file", "0 files contain the marker", f"{len(leaks)} of {len(enc)} files contain the marker", not leaks and len(enc) > 0, str(VAULT))
97# Join all encrypted files for one aggregate entropy measure.
98blob = b"".join(p.read_bytes() for p in enc)
99# Record the entropy result: random-looking data scores close to 8.0; this supports the conclusion but does not prove it alone.
100record("D3", "Ciphertext looks random (entropy)", ">= 7.90 bits/byte", f"{entropy(blob):.3f} bits/byte over {len(blob)} bytes", entropy(blob) >= 7.90, str(VAULT))
101# Record the check that only a person can perform with the real tool (VeraCrypt, BitLocker or LUKS): wrong passphrase refused, right passphrase opens.
102record("D4", "Wrong passphrase refused, right one opens", "refused / opens (screenshots)", "Lesson 1 run, steps 11 and 12 (or the tool's own screenshots)", None, "screenshots in CH6 evidence folder")
103 
104# Try a plain-HTTP request on port 80.
105try:
106    # Open a TCP connection to port 80 of the service, with a 5-second time limit.
107    with socket.create_connection((SVC_IP, 80), timeout=5) as s:
108        # Send a minimal HTTP/1.1 request for the root page, naming the service in the Host header.
109        s.sendall(f"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {SVC_NAME}\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n".encode())
110        # Read the beginning of the answer as text.
111        head = s.recv(2048).decode(errors="replace").split("\r\n")
112    # Keep the Location header of the answer (empty when there is none).
113    location = next((l for l in head if l.lower().startswith("location:")), "")
114    # Record: a 301 or 308 answer that points to an https:// address passes.
115    record("H1", "Port 80 never serves the page", "301/308 to https:// or port closed", f"{head[0]} | {location}", head[0].split()[1] in ("301", "308") and "https://" in location, f"live test {SVC_IP}:80")
116# A refused connection means that nothing listens on port 80, which also passes.
117except ConnectionRefusedError:
118    # Record the closed port.
119    record("H1", "Port 80 never serves the page", "301/308 to https:// or port closed", "connection refused (port closed)", True, f"live test {SVC_IP}:80")
120# Any other network error (time-out, no route) means the test could not run: record it as a failure.
121except OSError as e:
122    # Record the error as the observed result.
123    record("H1", "Port 80 never serves the page", "301/308 to https:// or port closed", f"test not possible: {e}", False, f"live test {SVC_IP}:80")
124 
125# Build a client context that trusts only the exported intranet certificate; this context also checks the host name.
126ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=CAFILE)
127# Read the fingerprint recorded in the device registry (Lesson 2, step h16), without colons and in lower case.
128registry_fp = next(csv.DictReader(open(REGISTRY_CSV)))["sha256_fingerprint"].replace(":", "").lower()
129# Try the TLS session; a network error or a failed certificate check is recorded instead of stopping the script.
130try:
131    # Open the TCP connection to port 443 and run the TLS handshake with the service name in SNI (Server Name Indication).
132    with socket.create_connection((SVC_IP, 443), timeout=5) as raw, ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=SVC_NAME) as tls:
133        # Note the negotiated protocol version and cipher suite.
134        version, cipher = tls.version(), tls.cipher()[0]
135        # Take the server certificate in binary DER form and compute its SHA-256 fingerprint.
136        seen_fp = hashlib.sha256(tls.getpeercert(binary_form=True)).hexdigest()
137        # Request the page inside the encrypted session.
138        tls.sendall(f"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {SVC_NAME}\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n".encode())
139        # Read the response headers.
140        resp = tls.recv(4096).decode(errors="replace").split("\r\n")
141# OSError covers refused or unreachable services and every TLS error, including a certificate that fails verification.
142except OSError as e:
143    # Record one failed row that explains why no HTTPS session could be established.
144    record("H2", "TLS session with the intranet", "session established", f"no session: {e}", False, f"live test {SVC_IP}:443")
145# The else block runs only when the session succeeded.
146else:
147    # Record the protocol version: only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 pass.
148    record("H2", "Negotiated protocol and cipher suite", "TLSv1.2 or TLSv1.3", f"{version}, {cipher}", version in ("TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"), f"live test {SVC_IP}:443")
149    # Record the fingerprint comparison: the certificate presented must be exactly the one in the registry.
150    record("H3", "Certificate = registry entry (SHA-256)", registry_fp[:16] + "...", seen_fp[:16] + "...", seen_fp == registry_fp, REGISTRY_CSV)
151    # Record the host-name check: reaching this line means the TLS library compared the name with the SAN and accepted it.
152    record("H4", "Host name verified against the SAN", f"{SVC_NAME} accepted", f"{resp[0]} (check_hostname={ctx.check_hostname})", ctx.check_hostname and " 200 " in resp[0], f"live test {SVC_IP}:443")
153    # Find the HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) header in the response.
154    hsts = next((l for l in resp if l.lower().startswith("strict-transport-security")), "absent")
155    # Record the HSTS result.
156    record("H5", "HSTS header present", "Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=...", hsts, hsts != "absent", f"live test {SVC_IP}:443")
157 
158# Split every IPv4 packet of the WAN capture into its parts.
159wan = [dissect(ip) for ip in packets(WAN_PCAP)]
160# Keep the WireGuard payloads: UDP with port 51820 on either side.
161wg = [p[3] for p in wan if p[0] == 17 and 51820 in (p[1], p[2])]
162# Count the four WireGuard message types: 1 = handshake initiation, 2 = handshake response, 3 = cookie reply, 4 = transport data (each starts with its type byte and three zero bytes).
163types = {t: sum(1 for m in wg if m[0] == t and m[1:4] == b"\0\0\0") for t in (1, 2, 3, 4)}
164# Record: an initiation, a response and transport data must all be present.
165record("V1", "WireGuard handshake and data on the WAN", "types 1 and 2 present, type 4 > 0", f"{len(wg)} messages: init {types[1]}, response {types[2]}, cookie {types[3]}, data {types[4]}", types[1] > 0 and types[2] > 0 and types[4] > 0, WAN_PCAP)
166# Record: no other IPv4 packet crossed the WAN interface during the test.
167record("V2", "Only WireGuard crossed the WAN", "0 other IPv4 packets", f"{len(wan) - len(wg)} other IPv4 packets", len(wan) == len(wg), WAN_PCAP)
168 
169# Search every WAN payload for the canary and for the service name.
170leak = any(CANARY in m or SVC_NAME.encode() in m for m in wg)
171# Record the leak test.
172record("V3", "Canary and service name absent on the WAN", "not found", "FOUND" if leak else "not found", not leak, WAN_PCAP)
173# Join the encrypted part of every transport message (everything after its 16-byte clear header).
174cipher_bytes = b"".join(m[16:] for m in wg if m[0] == 4)
175# Record the entropy of the encrypted payloads.
176record("V4", "Tunnel payload looks random (entropy)", ">= 7.90 bits/byte", f"{entropy(cipher_bytes):.3f} bits/byte over {len(cipher_bytes)} bytes", entropy(cipher_bytes) >= 7.90, WAN_PCAP)
177 
178# Split every IPv4 packet of the tunnel capture into its parts.
179inner = [dissect(ip) for ip in packets(TUNNEL_PCAP)]
180# Count the packets that carry the canary (sent in a plain-HTTP request inside the tunnel).
181canary_in = sum(1 for p in inner if CANARY in p[3])
182# Count the packets that carry the service name (sent in clear in the TLS ClientHello).
183name_in = sum(1 for p in inner if SVC_NAME.encode() in p[3])
184# Record: seeing the canary inside proves the test traffic really crossed the tunnel, so its absence on the WAN is meaningful.
185record("V5", "Canary visible inside the tunnel (positive control)", "found", f"canary in {canary_in} packets; service name in {name_in} packets", canary_in > 0, TUNNEL_PCAP)
186 
187# Keep the two status lines that prove a working tunnel.
188lines = [l.strip() for l in pathlib.Path(WG_SHOW).read_text().splitlines() if l.strip().startswith(("latest handshake", "transfer"))]
189# Record the tunnel status.
190record("V6", "Tunnel status on NM-FW01", "latest handshake + transfer", "; ".join(lines) or "absent", len(lines) == 2, WG_SHOW)
191 
192# Open the CSV file for writing.
193with open("C17_validation_evidence.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
194    # Prepare a writer that uses the keys of the first row as column names.
195    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(EVIDENCE[0]))
196    # Write the column names.
197    w.writeheader()
198    # Write one line per test.
199    w.writerows(EVIDENCE)
200# Build the Markdown version of the same table: a header line, a separator line, then one line per test.
201md = ["| Test | Check | Expected | Observed | Result | Evidence |", "|---|---|---|---|---|---|"] + [f"| {r['test']} | {r['check']} | {r['expected']} | {r['observed']} | {r['result']} | {r['source']} |" for r in EVIDENCE]
202# Write the Markdown file.
203pathlib.Path("C17_validation_evidence.md").write_text("\n".join(md) + "\n")
204# Count the verdicts.
205totals = {v: sum(1 for r in EVIDENCE if r["result"] == v) for v in ("PASS", "FAIL", "MANUAL")}
206# Print the totals and the names of the two files written.
207print(f"PASS {totals['PASS']} | FAIL {totals['FAIL']} | MANUAL {totals['MANUAL']} -> C17_validation_evidence.csv and C17_validation_evidence.md written")
208

How to run it, and what each step does

    
Run: On NM-RW01 (through the tunnel), with the vault from Example 1, the exported certificate and registry from Example 2, and the two capture files in the current directory: python3 nm_validate_encryption.py. It writes C17_validation_evidence.csv and .md. — Recorded 2026-10-10 11:57 UTC · Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (Linux 6.18.44-fc-v114) · Python 3.13.16 · OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024 · nginx version: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu) · wireguard-go v0.0.20230223 + wireguard-tools v1.0.20210914

    
  1. Step 1 (v1). Settings: what to test, and where the expected values come from.
  2. Step 2 (v2). Data at rest, positive control: the marker test must find the marker in the plaintext copy (proof the test works).
  3. Step 3 (v3). Data at rest: no encrypted file contains the marker, and the ciphertext entropy is close to 8 bits per byte.
  4. Step 4 (v4). HTTPS-only, test 1: port 80 must redirect to HTTPS or be closed - it must never return the page.
  5. Step 5 (v5). HTTPS-only, tests 2 to 5: TLS version, certificate against the registry, host-name check, HSTS header.
  6. Step 6 (v6). VPN: count the WireGuard messages captured on the WAN and confirm that nothing else crossed it.
  7. Step 7 (v7). VPN: the canary and the service name are invisible on the WAN, and the encrypted payload looks random.
  8. Step 8 (v8). VPN, positive control: the same canary IS visible on wg0, where the firewall has already decrypted the packets.
  9. Step 9 (v9). VPN status: the "wg show" output of NM-FW01 shows a recent handshake and transferred bytes.
  10. Step 10 (v10). Write the evidence table (CSV and Markdown) for section 6.4 of the Course Procedure Manual.

  

  
  
  

▣Diagrams and figures for this lesson
🂠Flashcards — five per sub-topic
Click a card to reveal the answer on its back.
3.1 — Why validation is a step of its own
Concept 1
Why is validation a separate step from configuration?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
A checkbox, a padlock or 'connected' are claims, not evidence, and each has failed silently. Validation confirms with a repeatable test that the control works, and keeps the result for a second person to check.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What are the four parts of a good validation, in order?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Expected (written first from the design), test (one repeatable test), observed (recorded exactly), and evidence (a capture, screenshot or export, named and dated). This is section 6.4 of the manual.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What is a positive control, with an example?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The same test run where the answer must be 'yes' — e.g. the marker is found in the plaintext copy. It proves the test works, so a 'not found' on the ciphertext is meaningful.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What is a negative test, and when is it a pass?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Trying what must fail and recording the failure — wrong passphrase refused, untrusted client refused, HTTP gets no page. A failure that was expected is a pass.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
Why write the expected result before running the test?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
So the test cannot be bent to fit whatever happens. The expected result comes from the design, and the observed result is then compared honestly against it.
◂ click to flip back
3.2 — Validating data at rest
Concept 1
What is the marker test for data at rest?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
A unique string (NORTHMAPLE-CONFIDENTIAL) is placed in the plaintext and searched for in the encrypted files: found in the plaintext (positive control), absent from the ciphertext.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What does entropy measure, and what are the telling values?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The average information per byte, in bits. Encrypted data scores near the maximum 8.0 (recorded ~7.99); readable text scores about 4.6–4.8.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
Why can't high entropy alone prove encryption?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Compressed data also scores high. Entropy supports the conclusion but is used alongside the marker test, never instead of it.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What is the strongest data-at-rest validation, and who performs it?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Trying the wrong passphrase (refused) and the right one (files open and match) in the real tool — only a person can do it. A screenshot of both is the primary evidence.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
In the recorded run, what did the marker test show?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The marker was found in 3 of 3 plaintext files and in 0 of 3 encrypted files; the aggregate ciphertext entropy was about 7.99 bits per byte.
◂ click to flip back
3.3 — Validating HTTPS
Concept 1
What is the negative test for an HTTPS-only service?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Request the page over plain HTTP and confirm a redirect, never the page. In the recorded run port 80 answered 301 Moved Permanently to the https:// address.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
How do you confirm the server presents the right certificate?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
Compare the SHA-256 fingerprint of the certificate it presents against the device registry line; they must match byte for byte. The recorded fingerprint matched.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
Why does the host-name check during validation depend on Lesson 2?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The TLS library accepts the certificate only because the typed name is in the SAN. A correct SAN (set in Lesson 2) is what makes the host-name validation pass.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What did the recorded TLS validation observe?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
TLS 1.3 with TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, the presented certificate matching the registry fingerprint, the host name verified against the SAN, and the HSTS header present.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
Which tools list every protocol and cipher a service accepts?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
testssl.sh and nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script, used to confirm that TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are refused; openssl s_client reports the version, cipher and certificate of a live service.
◂ click to flip back
3.4 — Validating the tunnel
Concept 1
What is the decisive test that a tunnel encrypts?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
A packet capture at two points, compared: the firewall's WAN interface (what the Internet carries) and the tunnel interface wg0 (after decryption).
◂ click to flip back
Concept 2
What is the canary, and how is it used in the two captures?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
A unique string (NM-CANARY-1710) sent through the tunnel during the capture. It must be absent on the WAN and present on wg0 — the positive control proving the test traffic used the tunnel.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 3
What did the WAN capture show in the recorded run?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
34 WireGuard messages (1 handshake initiation, 1 response, 32 transport-data) and nothing else — no HTTP, TLS or DNS; the canary and service name were not found; entropy ~7.97.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 4
What does 'wg show' provide as evidence, and what does it never print?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
The latest handshake time and the bytes transferred per peer (recorded: handshake 3 seconds ago, ~2.7 KiB in / 3.9 KiB out). It never prints a private key.
◂ click to flip back
Concept 5
Where are the packet-capture tools in pfSense and OPNsense?
click to reveal ▸
Answer
pfSense: Diagnostics > Packet Capture. OPNsense: Interfaces > Diagnostics > Packet capture. Both download a capture file you open in Wireshark.
◂ click to flip back
✎Practice — 4 MCQ and 2 MSQ
Choose your answer(s), use the hint if needed, then reveal the answer and the explanation. MCQ = one answer; MSQ = several answers (the number is shown).



  
MCQone answer

  
1. Why is a green padlock in the browser not sufficient evidence that the service is HTTPS-only?

  
It is a claim, not a repeatable test with recorded evidence a second person can check
A padlock only appears on internal sites
A padlock proves TLS 1.0 is in use
The padlock disables the SAN check

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Think about the difference between believing a control works and proving it.

  
A padlock is a claim; validation requires a repeatable test, the observed result recorded, and evidence kept for a second person to verify — for example that port 80 only redirects. The other options are simply false statements about what a padlock means.





  
MCQone answer

  
2. In the two-point capture test, what proves that the tunnel is actually encrypting the traffic?

  
The canary is absent on the WAN capture but present on the wg0 capture
The WAN capture contains more packets than the wg0 capture
The wg0 capture is larger than the WAN capture in bytes
Both captures show the canary in plaintext

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. One capture point is before decryption, the other after; the canary ties them together.

  
The canary must be unreadable on the WAN (encrypted) and readable on wg0 (after the firewall decrypts), which proves the test traffic really crossed the tunnel and was encrypted on the untrusted side. The byte or packet counts (2–3) are not the proof, and the canary appearing on the WAN (4) would mean the opposite — no encryption.





  
MCQone answer

  
3. During HTTPS validation, the host-name check passes. Which earlier choice made that possible?

  
The certificate's SAN was set to the service name in Lesson 2
The private key was set to mode 600
The certificate was given 200 days of validity
HSTS was added to the response

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. The host-name check compares the typed name against one certificate field.

  
The TLS library accepts the certificate only because the typed name is in the SAN, which was set correctly when the certificate was created. Key permissions (2), validity length (3) and HSTS (4) are all good practice but none of them is what the host-name check compares against.





  
MCQone answer

  
4. Why does the validator place the marker in the plaintext and confirm it is found there first?

  
As a positive control proving the search works, so 'not found' in the ciphertext is meaningful
To add entropy to the plaintext files
Because the marker is the encryption key
To make the ciphertext files larger

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. A test that can never say 'yes' proves nothing when it says 'no'.

  
Finding the marker in the plaintext is the positive control: it shows the search actually works, so its absence from the ciphertext is real evidence rather than a broken test. The marker is not a key (3), is not there to change entropy (2) or size (4).





  
MSQ (Select 3)Select 3

  
5. Which statements about the structure of a good validation are correct? (Select 3)

  
The expected result is written before the test, from the design
A negative test records an expected failure, which counts as a pass
Evidence is kept, named and dated, for a second person to check
The observed result should be summarized in your own words, not copied
A test with no positive control is always the strongest kind
Writing the expected result after the test keeps it objective

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Three describe the expected/test/observed/evidence discipline; three invert it.

  
Correct: expected written first from the design (1); a negative test's expected failure is a pass (2); evidence is kept, named and dated (3). Wrong: the observed result is copied exactly, not paraphrased (4); a positive control makes a test stronger, not weaker (5); writing the expected result after the test lets it be bent to fit (6).





  
MSQ (Select 4)Select 4

  
6. In the recorded tunnel validation, which observations were part of the evidence? (Select 4)

  
The WAN carried only WireGuard messages — no HTTP, TLS or DNS
The canary was not found on the WAN capture
wg show reported a recent handshake and bytes transferred
The encrypted WAN payload measured about 7.97 bits per byte of entropy
wg show printed the peers' private keys for the record
The service name was found in clear on the WAN capture

  

    
    
    
  

  
Hint. Two options describe things that must never happen if the tunnel is working and safe.

  
Correct: only WireGuard on the WAN (1); canary absent on the WAN (2); wg show gave a recent handshake and transfer (3); WAN payload entropy ~7.97 (4). Wrong: wg show never prints private keys (5); the service name being readable on the WAN (6) would mean the tunnel was NOT encrypting.

LAB_06 Part 2 — summary (built separately)
LAB_06 is performed today, Class 17. Part 1 (the remote-access tunnel) was prepared in Class 16; Part 2 (encryption and validation) applies all three of today's lessons. This page only summarizes what the lab will ask — the complete lab kit is distributed in the work period and is built as a separate document.
Part 1 — remote-access tunnel
  • A remote-access VPN tunnel into NorthMaple's network on NM-FW01: WireGuard recommended (pfSense CE (Community Edition) (Community Edition) package or OPNsense core), OpenVPN or the built-in IPsec accepted with the substitution stated in writing (Final Project, section 1.8).
  • Keys, users and allowed networks configured as in Class 16: one key pair for the remote worker NM-RW01, tunnel address 10.66.0.2, least-privilege rules on the tunnel interface.
  • The remote worker connects through the simulated Internet and the connection is verified.
Part 2 — encryption and validation
  • One folder or volume of company data encrypted with a free tool, data at rest (Lesson 1).
  • HTTPS enabled with a self-signed certificate on one internal service (Lesson 2).
  • Validation that the tunnel traffic is encrypted, the service answers only over HTTPS, and the encrypted data cannot be opened without its key (Lesson 3).
Before the lab
  • NM-FW01 from LAB_05 runs; take a snapshot before you start.
  • NM-LX01 ready to clone into NM-RW01; the NAT network for the simulated Internet exists.
  • The Course Procedure Manual holds an empty Chapter 6 with headings 6.1 to 6.6.

Appendix — the four-question check for any source
  1. Who published it, and what do they sell? Not disqualifying — vendor research is often excellent — but it changes how you read the conclusion.
  2. Is there a primary source? A statistic with no linked methodology is a marketing figure. Follow it back or discard it.
  3. What is the date, and does the date matter for this claim? Certificate lifetimes changed in 2026 and change again in 2027: an older post can be correct for its year and wrong today.
  4. Does it agree with a standards body? If a claim contradicts NIST, CIS or the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, it needs much stronger evidence than a confident tone.

Legal Notice, Disclaimer, and Acceptable Use Policy — Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) — Version 1.0, effective August 29, 2026 — Cyber.SoHo. The provisions below govern every part of this material; the most relevant are also woven into the opening, the videos and the LAB_06 summary above.
§1. Plain-Language Summary
This document protects everyone: the students, the viewers, and the author. In short: all the material of this course is provided for education only. You may practice the activities only inside your own, isolated laboratory environment, or on systems for which you hold explicit written permission. You are fully and solely responsible for your own actions, your equipment, your accounts, your costs, and your time. By reading, watching, downloading, or using any part of the material, you accept this entire document.
§2. Educational Purpose Only
All lectures, labs, projects, quizzes, exams, documents, videos, and social-media publications of the course Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) (together, "the Material") are created for one purpose: teaching defensive cybersecurity to adult learners of the Cybersecurity AEC (Attestation d'études collégiales) program. The Material shows how to protect systems, not how to attack the systems of others. Nothing in the Material is an invitation, an instruction, or an authorization to access, test, or damage any real system, network, account, or data.
§3. Acceptable Use and Prohibited Actions (Student Warning)
You may: practice only inside your personal, isolated laboratory environment, as defined in LAB_01: a local virtualization tool (for example VirtualBox) or your own personal free-tier cloud account on AWS (Amazon Web Services) or Microsoft Azure; practice on any other system only if you hold explicit written permission from the owner of that system, obtained before you start; use snapshots and isolated virtual networks so that a mistake stays inside your laboratory. You must never: scan, probe, attack, intercept, monitor, or access any system, network, wireless network, or account that is not yours — including those of the college, an employer, a business, a public website, or a neighbor; create, install, or release malicious software outside your isolated laboratory; attempt password, credential, or interception attacks against any real account or any real communication; use the Material, or any tool presented in it, to break any law or any policy that applies to you. Cloud responsibilities: if you use a cloud account, you must respect the acceptable-use policies of the provider (AWS or Microsoft Azure). Free tiers have limits; monitor them. All cloud costs, overage charges, and account consequences are your responsibility.
§4. Legal Warning
Unauthorized computer access or use is a criminal offence. In Canada, the Criminal Code contains, among other provisions: section 342.1 (unauthorized use of a computer), section 342.2 (possession of a device to obtain unauthorized use of a computer), and section 430(1.1) (mischief in relation to computer data). Penalties can include imprisonment. If you are located outside Canada, the laws of your own country, province, or state apply to you, and you must know and obey them. The policies and codes of conduct of your college apply in addition to the law. The instructor never asks for, and never authorizes, any illegal act. If an activity seems to touch a system you do not own, stop and ask the instructor before doing anything.

A link in the Material is not an endorsement.
§11. Ethics and Responsible Conduct
The course teaches defensive ("white-hat") cybersecurity. By using the Material, students agree to use their skills only to protect, never to harm, and to respect the privacy of others. If a student accidentally discovers a real vulnerability, the student reports it responsibly to the owner of the system and to the instructor, instead of exploiting it or publishing it. Academic integrity applies at all times, including the course rule on AI (Artificial Intelligence): any use of an AI tool in a submission must state the LLM (Large Language Model) used and the exact prompt(s) given to it.
§12. Social-Media Notice
Clips, posts, shorts, and videos published on public platforms (for example YouTube or TikTok) are educational demonstrations performed inside an isolated laboratory. Do not reproduce them outside such a laboratory. Third-party comments, re-uploads, edits, reactions, and translations are not verified and not endorsed by Cyber.SoHo, and they remain the sole responsibility of their authors. The terms of service and the community rules of each platform apply on that platform.
§13. Indemnification
By using the Material, you agree to indemnify and hold harmless Cyber.SoHo and the instructor from any claim, demand, damage, loss, or expense (including reasonable legal fees) resulting from your own actions or omissions, from your violation of this document, or from your violation of any law or of any right of a third party.
§14. Privacy
The Material itself collects no personal data. When an enrolled student signs the separate "Acknowledgment and Agreement" page, the student's name, the session number, the date, and a verification code are recorded in the course signature log; the drawn signature image stays only inside the record file that the student downloads and submits, and it is not published. If the signature log is hosted in a public repository, the log is publicly visible; hosting it in a private repository is recommended. On public platforms (for example YouTube or TikTok), the privacy policy of the platform applies.
§15. Governing Law, Severability, and Updates
This document is governed by the laws applicable in the Province of Quebec, Canada. If a court finds one clause invalid, the other clauses remain in force. Cyber.SoHo may update this document at any time; the current version, identified by its version number, replaces all previous versions. Before this document is reused or republished outside the course, a review by a lawyer licensed in the Province of Quebec is recommended.
§16. Acknowledgment and Acceptance
Reading, watching, downloading, or using any part of the Material means that you have read, understood, and accepted this entire document. Enrolled students also confirm their acceptance electronically: at the beginning of each session, they sign the separate "Acknowledgment and Agreement" page (Acknowledgment_and_Agreement_eSign.html), which creates their personal electronic signature record for that session.
